name: Miani
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.note: Only Z'graggen 1971/1980 survey wordlists and Pick 2020 subgrouping pp.188-194 found; no phonology/stress description located online.

new_statements.quote: In all four languages stress is contrastive and thus phonemic. Examples of contrastive stress are as follows: [...] Miani /'uŋu/ 'ripe' /u'ŋu/ 'red' /ga'gatob/ 'to take it down' /'gagatob/ 'to look at' /'uřam/ 'his stomach' /u'řam/ 'basket' [...] An interesting feature of stress has been noted in comparing two syllable words that are similar in all four languages. Maia tends to stress the first syllable, whereas Maiani, Miani and Mala stress the second syllable. /'arop/ 'three' (Maia) /a'řop/ 'three' (Maiani, Miani) /ŋga'řop/ 'three' (Mala) /'ulum/ 'dirty' (Maia) /u'lum/ 'dirty' (Maiani, Mala) /u'řum/ 'dirty' (Miani)
new_statements.citation: May, Jean & Eunice Loeweke. 1985 [dated February 1982]. A Recommended Alphabet for Maiani, Miani, Mala and Maia - Four Languages of the Kaukambaran Language Family. In John M. Clifton (ed.), Five phonological studies (Workpapers in Papua New Guinea Languages 31), 1-25. Ukarumpa: Summer Institute of Linguistics.
new_statements.locator: Section 4 'Stress', pp. 11-12 (PDF pp. 11-12); corroborated verbatim by May 1994/2004, Organised Phonology Data: Miani (Tani, Miani North) Language [PLA], p. 3 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)'.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is phonemic (contrastive) in Miani: word-level minimal pairs differ only in whether the first or second syllable is stressed (e.g. 'uŋu 'ripe' vs u'ŋu 'red'; 'gagatob 'to look at' vs ga'gatob 'to take it down'). No placement rule is given; the only generalisation is a cross-language observation that in comparable disyllables Miani (like Maiani and Mala) stresses the second syllable, whereas Maia stresses the first. The 1994 OPD repeats the same three pairs (spelled 'unu/u'nu, ga'gatow/'gagatow, 'uram/u'ram) and adds that phonemic stress is not written.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated as exceptions; the second-syllable pattern is offered as a tendency in disyllables, not a rule, and the minimal pairs show both first- and second-syllable stress. One pair ('uřam 'his stomach' vs u'řam 'basket') is plausibly morphological (u- 'his' prefix), as in sister language Maia where person prefixes carry stress contrasts.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms in a phonology/orthography sketch (isolated words); the OPD's allophony note refers to 'unstressed syllables' within the word. No phrase-level or intonation statement; no tone or length contrast reported.
new_statements.identity_note: Sources describe Miani proper [pla] = Z'graggen's 'Tani' northern part (OPD title: 'Miani (Tani, Miani North)'; villages Yoro, Suwat, Mugumat). May & Loeweke's Miani examples come from main-dialect speakers (Andrew Gai, Jacob Kulilain); they note a small coastal Miani dialect differing in consonants (/d/, /l/ for main-dialect /ʒ/) but say nothing about its stress. The OPD's running header reads 'Miani (Pila, Coastal Maia) OPD', a template artifact - the title page, villages and data are Miani. Sister variety Maiani [tnh] (maia1253, 'Miani South') is covered by the same 1985 paper (Maiani pairs 'apa/a'pa) but is a separate Glottolog language.

sources.note: 'Stress is contrastive and thus phonemic. Examples are as follows: 'unu 'ripe' / u'nu 'red'; ga'gatow 'to take it down' / 'gagatow 'to look at'; 'uram 'his stomach' / u'ram 'basket'.' Also: '/r/ is flap [ɾ] when occurring between vowels in unstressed syllables'; 'Phonemic stress is not written.' No tone or length contrast listed.

sources.citation: Pick, Andrew. 2020. A Reconstruction of Proto-Northern Adelbert Phonology and Lexicon. PhD dissertation, University of Hawai'i at Manoa. 485 pp. (Glottolog: subgrouping pp. 188-194; sec. 5.3.1 'Miani phonology' pp. 168-169; stress overview pp. 31-32.)
sources.note: Nothing on Miani stress: the Miani phonology section gives only the consonant inventory and t~s alternation. General remark pp. 31-32: 'Suprasegmental phonology, including stress, has only been described for a small number of Northern Adelbert languages' (Mauwake second-syllable per Berghäll 2015; Pamosu per Tupper 2012; Usan phonemic per Reesink 1987) and 'the available data on stress in most languages are minimal or nonexistent'.
